* Narration

** 1. Every time you lift your head  (0:00, 1:15)

/On screen:/
- /"Every time you lift your head, you slow down."/
- Ruby 4.0 ships *two* just-in-time compilers. Why build the second one?

/Say:/

[STORY: learning long-distance open water. Suggested shape: "When I started
swimming long distance I tried to go faster by pulling harder. I burned
out. My coach said: every time you lift your head, you slow down. Long
distance isn't about power. It's about not wasting any."]

That turns out to be how compilers make Ruby fast too: not by doing each
step harder, but by wasting less.

Ruby 4.0 came out last Christmas with two just-in-time compilers. YJIT has
made real Rails apps faster for years. ZJIT is new: Ruby's release notes call it "the next
generation of YJIT". And 4.1 ships in a few weeks. Most of us will upgrade without ever looking
at what changed.

So why build a second one? We'll follow one five-line method through
both, and by the end you'll see the exact line where one compiler has to
stop and the other doesn't. And next time someone says "Ruby is slow",
you'll have a better question to ask.

[Bio, one line: fifteen years of Ruby; I write Rust, which both are
written in.]

/Next: Ruby swims with its head up/

** 2. Ruby swims with its head up  (1:15, 0:15)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/head-up.svg: The beginner swimmer lifts their head every stroke

/Say:/

A beginner lifts their head every stroke: where am I, is this still right?
Safe, and slow.

Ruby's interpreter runs your code a lot like that. Let me show you.

/Next: Our five lines/

** 3. Our five lines  (1:30, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- code:
#+begin_example
class Point
  attr_reader :x, :y
  def initialize(x, y) = (@x, @y = x, y)
end
#+end_example
- code:
#+begin_example
def distance(a, b)
  dx = a.x - b.x
  dy = a.y - b.y
  Math.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)
end
#+end_example

/Say:/

Here's the method we'll follow all talk: the distance between two points.

Before any JIT touches it, Ruby turns it into bytecode, and the
interpreter runs that.

/Next: The bytecode/

** 4. The bytecode  (2:00, 1:00)

/On screen:/
- code:
#+begin_example
ruby -r ./distance -e 'puts RubyVM::InstructionSequence.of(method(:distance)).disasm'
#+end_example
- listing (captures/yarv-distance.txt):
#+begin_example
0000 getlocal_WC_0          a@0
0002 opt_send_without_block <calldata!mid:x, argc:0, ARGS_SIMPLE>
0004 getlocal_WC_0          b@1
0006 opt_send_without_block <calldata!mid:x, argc:0, ARGS_SIMPLE>
0008 opt_minus              <calldata!mid:-, argc:1, ARGS_SIMPLE>
0010 setlocal_WC_0          dx@2
 ...
0040 opt_send_without_block <calldata!mid:sqrt, argc:1, ARGS_SIMPLE>
0042 leave
#+end_example
- Ruby 4.1.0-preview1

/Say:/

[Run the live block.]

Top to bottom: get a, call x on it. Get b, call x on it. Minus. Store it
in dx.

That "minus" doesn't know it's subtracting numbers. It could be anything
with a minus method. There's a fast path for plain numbers, but it has to
check first, every single time: the interpreter lifting its head. You can run this line on your own code tonight.

/Next: Learning to sight/

** 5. Learning to sight  (3:00, 1:00)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/sighting.svg: A trained swimmer looks once, then keeps their head down

/Say:/

[STORY, one or two lines: learning to sight. You still have to look, or
you swim the wrong way. The skill is looking less, and only when it
counts.]

A just-in-time compiler does that for your busiest code. It looks once
per stretch, not every stroke: a quick check called a guard, "is this
still a number?", then a run of fast machine code. If the check fails, it falls back to the careful way.

Ruby has two of them, and they look in different ways.

/Next: YJIT: compile as you go/

** 6. YJIT: compile as you go  (4:00, 0:45)

/On screen:/
- Once a method is warm, compile a small piece, run it
- Look at the values that really turned up
- Compile the next piece for exactly those
- listing (captures/yjit-distance.txt):
#+begin_example
# Insn: 0002 opt_send_without_block (stack_size: 1)
# call to Point#x
# guard not immediate
# guard known class
# guard shape
# Block: distance@distance.rb:7
# Insn: 0004 getlocal_WC_0 (stack_size: 1)
# defer_compilation
#+end_example
- Ruby 4.1.0-preview1 · ~ruby --yjit --yjit-dump-disasm~

/Say:/

YJIT compiles as it goes. This is its own commentary, machine code taken
out.

At a.x it checks: a real object, a Point, laid out as before. Then it
reads @x directly.

"defer_compilation" means: stop here, let the code run, and compile the
next piece when we get there, for whatever value is really there. So it
only compiles code that actually runs, for the values that actually turn
up.

[Depth: lazy basic block versioning. "Shape" is an object's
instance-variable layout.]

/Next: ZJIT: watch, then plan/

** 7. ZJIT: watch, then plan  (4:45, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- While the interpreter runs the method, record which types turn up: a *profile*
- Then turn the *whole method* into a plan: the *IR* (intermediate representation)
- Improve the plan, then compile it, once

/Say:/

ZJIT does it the other way round. While the interpreter runs your method,
it keeps notes on which types showed up. That's a profile.

Then it turns the whole method into a plan, its intermediate
representation, improves the plan, and compiles it in one go.

/Next: ZJIT: the IR on one slide/

** 8. ZJIT: the IR on one slide  (5:15, 1:00)

/On screen:/
- listing (captures/zjit-distance.txt):
#+begin_example
fn distance@distance.rb:7:
bb3(v15:BasicObject, v16:BasicObject, v17:BasicObject):
  v79:ObjectSubclass[class_exact:Point] = GuardType v16
  v82:CShape[0x10007a] = GuardBitEquals v81, CShape(0x10007a) recompile
  v83:BasicObject = LoadField v79, :@x
  ...
  v93:Fixnum = GuardType v83, Fixnum recompile
  v94:Fixnum = GuardType v90, Fixnum
  v95:Fixnum = FixnumSub v93, v94
  ...
  v118:Fixnum = FixnumMult v95, v95
  ...
  v130:BasicObject = CCallWithFrame v54, :Math.sqrt, v126
  Return v130
#+end_example
- The whole method as one plan. ~GuardType~ and ~GuardBitEquals~ are sights. ~v95~ is ~dx~.
- Ruby 4.1.0-preview1 · ~ruby --zjit --zjit-dump-hir~

/Say:/

This is ZJIT's plan for our five lines. The whole method fits on one
slide.

Read one line and you can read them all. "v95, colon, Fixnum, equals,
FixnumSub v93, v94": a name, its type, then the operation and its inputs.

Every value gets a name, set exactly once. v16 is a. GuardType: is it a
Point? GuardBitEquals: laid out as expected? The same checks YJIT made.

FixnumSub makes dx, named v95. Then dx times dx: FixnumMult v95, v95. And
CCallWithFrame calls into C for Math.sqrt. Neither compiler sees inside
that C code.

[Depth: "set once" is SSA. Trimmed: PatchPoints, which discard this code
if someone redefines Point#x.]

/Next: On five lines, a tie/

** 9. On five lines, a tie  (6:15, 0:45)

/On screen:/
- listing (captures/yjit-distance.txt, zjit-distance.txt):
#+begin_example
YJIT                                         ZJIT
# Insn: 0028 getlocal_WC_0 (stack_size: 2)   v95:Fixnum = FixnumSub v93, v94
# Insn: 0030 opt_mult (stack_size: 3)        ...
# Insn: 0032 getlocal_WC_0 (stack_size: 2)   v118:Fixnum = FixnumMult v95, v95
#+end_example
- At ~dx * dx~ neither checks again: both already know ~dx~ is a number. Nearly a tie.
- Ruby 4.1.0-preview1 · default settings

/Say:/

So who wins on our five lines? Honestly: nearly nobody.

At dx times dx, YJIT doesn't check again. It carried "dx is a number"
forward from the minus. ZJIT doesn't either. ZJIT is slightly ahead: it
doesn't re-check a and b before reading y. But it's small.

On straight-line code like this one, YJIT already gets the wins. To see why
ZJIT exists, we need something every Ruby codebase is full of.

/Next: The plateau/

** 10. The plateau  (7:00, 1:00)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/plateau.svg: Swim times drop fast while learning to sight, then stop moving

/Say:/

[STORY: the plateau. Suggested: "Sighting made me faster every week. Then
it stopped. When I looked at where the time went, the straight legs were
fine. I was losing it at the turns." Keep only what's true for you.]

The ZJIT team built ZJIT, in their words, to "raise the performance
ceiling". Here's one place you can see what they mean: the turns. In Ruby, a turn
is a method call, and we write small methods calling small methods.
That's how we're taught.

That's my plateau, not YJIT's report card: this is about how high a
design can go.

Let's add one turn to our five lines.

/Next: One more call/

** 11. One more call  (8:00, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- code:
#+begin_example
def sq(n) = n * n

def distance(a, b)
  dx = a.x - b.x
  dy = a.y - b.y
  Math.sqrt(sq(dx) + sq(dy))
end
#+end_example

/Say:/

The smallest refactor you'd ever make: pull n times n into a helper
called sq.

/Next: One more call is one more buoy/

** 12. One more call is one more buoy  (8:30, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/turn-buoy.svg: One more call is one more turn buoy

/Say:/

YJIT reaches the turn and has to make the call: sq is separate machine
code.

ZJIT can see the whole course, turn included. It splices sq into
distance. That's called inlining.

/Next: At the turn buoy/

** 13. At the turn buoy  (9:00, 1:30)

/On screen:/
- listing (captures/yjit-sq.txt, zjit-sq.txt):
#+begin_example
YJIT                                     ZJIT
# call to Object#sq                      v95:Fixnum = FixnumSub v93, v94
# push callee control frame              ...
# gen_direct_jmp: existing block         PushInlineFrame :sq, v116, num_args=1
 ...                                     v169:Fixnum = FixnumMult v95, v95
# Block: sq@distance_sq.rb:6             PopInlineFrame
# Insn: 0004 opt_mult (stack_size: 2)
# guard arg0 fixnum
# guard arg1 fixnum
# pop stack frame
 ...                                     ...
# Insn: 0036 opt_plus (stack_size: 3)    v125:Fixnum = FixnumAdd v169, v173
# guard arg0 fixnum
#+end_example
- YJIT: a real call into a general ~sq~, and a check again when it returns. ZJIT: ~sq~ spliced in. No jump, no check on ~n~, and it knows the result is a number.
- Ruby 4.1.0-preview1 · default settings

/Say:/

Here's the turn, in each compiler's own words.

YJIT, left. It compiles sq as its own code, so distance has to call it.

A call isn't free. Save where you are, set up a new frame for sq, jump
there, run it, tear the frame down, jump back. All of that to multiply two
numbers. Since that sq serves every caller, it checks n. And when it
returns, YJIT doesn't know what came back, so at the plus it checks again.

ZJIT, right. sq is spliced in: no jump, no check on n. It still sets up a
light frame, in case it ever has to hand back to the interpreter. And
because it saw inside sq, it knows the result is a number: the plus has no
check at all.

[Fair to YJIT, if asked: force it to compile early and it carries "n is a
number" into sq, so no check there. Its team says its design "allows for
easy interprocedural type-based specialization". The call stays. Also if
asked: ZJIT's inline frame is real (stack check, save SP, push frame); it
is cheaper than a call, not free.]

/Next: Why it's a ceiling/

** 14. Why it's a ceiling  (10:30, 1:15)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/ceiling.svg: YJIT compiles pieces as it goes; ZJIT builds one plan for the whole method and can rewrite it

/Say:/

So why can't YJIT just do what ZJIT did? Because of its shape.

YJIT turns each piece into machine code as soon as it reaches it. There's
never a picture of the whole method, so there's nothing to rearrange
afterwards. It can fold in the tiniest things, like the attribute reader we saw.
But in every capture in this talk, a method doing real work, sq,
convert_key, double, stays a real call. And after the call returns, YJIT
checks the result again.

ZJIT builds the whole method as a plan first. And a plan can be rewritten
before it runs: splice a small method in, then drop the checks on both
sides of it, because the plan can see what goes in and what comes out.

That's the ceiling. In the ZJIT team's words: instead of one piece at a
time, one entire method at a time, which gives the optimizer more code to
work with.

[If asked "doesn't YJIT have an IR?": yes, a low-level one inside its code
generator (yjit/src/backend/ir.rs). What it doesn't build is a plan of a
whole method.]

[Sources: Bernstein, Rails at Scale, 2025-05-14: "Instead of compiling one
basic block at a time, it compiles one entire method at a time"; "gives
more code at once to the optimizer".]

/Next: The 2-beat kick/

** 15. The 2-beat kick  (11:45, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/two-beat-kick.svg: The 2-beat kick is timed to the whole stroke

/Say:/

[STORY, short: the 2-beat kick. "Fewer kicks, timed to the whole stroke.
I couldn't get there one kick at a time."]

Same with sq: you can only splice it in if you can see the caller and the
callee together.

/Next: So, why build the second one?/

** 16. So, why build the second one?  (12:15, 1:00)

/On screen:/
- 1. The next gains need the *whole method as one plan*. A compiler that works piece by piece never has one.
- 2. A more traditional compiler, so *more people can help build it*.
- quote: "we want to both raise the performance ceiling (bigger compilation unit size and SSA IR) and encourage more outside contribution (by becoming a more traditional method compiler)." --- Max Bernstein, ZJIT team, Rails at Scale, 2025-12-24 
- Source: railsatscale.com/2025-12-24-launch-zjit

/Say:/

Back to the question I started with: why build a second one?

Because the next gains, like seeing through that call, need the whole
method as one plan, and a compiler that works piece by piece never has
one. And because a traditional compiler shape lets more people help.
In their words:

It isn't free. ZJIT plans from what it saw while warming up. If your
traffic changes after that, the plan is wrong: it falls back, then
recompiles from a new profile. YJIT adds another version on the spot, up
to a limit (four by default).

[Sources for the limit: YJIT's max_versions option, default 4,
yjit/src/options.rs. "recompile" is marked on ZJIT's guards in every HIR
capture.]

[Sources: launch post 2025-12-24 ("if your method call patterns change
significantly after your code has been compiled, we will frequently
side-exit into the interpreter"); merge post 2025-05-14 ("a more
traditional “textbook” compiler so it is easy for the community to
contribute to").]

def [](key)

/Say:/

Toy methods flatter compilers. Here's one you run right now:
HashWithIndifferentAccess, which Rails params are built on. Look up a key:
turn a symbol into a string, then a normal hash lookup. And look: a small
method calling a small method.

** 18. params, through both  (13:45, 0:45)

/On screen:/
- YJIT at ~[]~:
- listing (captures/hwia-yjit-disasm.txt):
#+begin_example
# call to ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess#convert_key
# push callee control frame

#+end_example
- ZJIT at ~[]~:
- listing (captures/hwia-zjit-hir.txt):

The same turn, in real code.

YJIT makes a real call into convert_key, just like sq.

ZJIT splices convert_key in. "Symbol triple-equals key" becomes a plain
type test and a branch. Then both compilers call Hash#[], which is written
in C.

[Depth: where the caller passes a literal like :id, ZJIT inlines [] and
convert_key into it and folds "Symbol === :id" away entirely.]

/Next: The feed stop/

** 19. The feed stop  (14:30, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- diagram img/out/feed-stop.svg: A feed stop: a better stroke doesn't make it shorter

/Say:/

And that's the feed stop. Hashing the key and finding it happens in C, and
no Ruby compiler speeds up the C itself. Same for waiting on the database, and for
garbage collection. A better stroke doesn't shorten the stop at the boat.

/Next: A glimpse: seven everyday lines/

** 20. A glimpse: seven everyday lines  (15:00, 0:45)

/On screen:/
- Each line in its own method, called 100,000 times, default settings. Counting calls into Ruby methods: calls into C happen under both.

| One line | YJIT: real calls into Ruby methods | ZJIT: inlined into one plan |
|----------+------------------------------------+-----------------------------|
| =params[:name].present?= | 4 calls | all 4 inlined |
| =name.presence= | 3 calls | all 3 inlined |
| =text.squish= | 2 calls | both inlined |
| =list.second= | 1 call | 1 inlined |
| =5.minutes= | 3 calls | 2 inlined, 1 call |
| =obj.try(:upcase)= | 1 call | 1 call (not inlined) |
| =nil.blank?= | inlined | folded to a constant |

- Fewer jumps and fewer checks, not free: ZJIT still sets up a light frame for each. We counted calls; we didn't time them.
- activesupport 8.1.4.1 · Ruby 4.1.0-preview1 · default settings

/Say:/

params isn't a one-off. Seven lines you'll find in any Rails app.

Five of them: YJIT makes real calls, ZJIT turns them into one plan. But
read the bottom too. 5.minutes still calls initialize. try isn't inlined
at all. And nil.blank? YJIT inlines that one as well.

And inlined isn't free: ZJIT still sets up a light frame for each. We
counted calls. We didn't time them.

/Next: Calm water, choppy water/

** 21. Calm water, choppy water  (15:45, 1:15)

/On screen:/
- code:
#+begin_example
def double(x) = x + x   # called with Integers only, or with five types
#+end_example
- Calm, ZJIT: spliced in, one check, one add.
- listing (captures/zjit-calm.txt):
#+begin_example
v44:Fixnum = GuardType v10, Fixnum recompile
v46:Fixnum = FixnumAdd v44, v44
#+end_example
- Choppy: five types.
- listing (captures/yjit-choppy.txt, zjit-choppy.txt):
#+begin_example
YJIT                        ZJIT
# guard arg0 fixnum         CondBranchHasType v10, Fixnum, bb12(), bb13()
# call to Float#+           v79:BasicObject = CCallWithFrame v47, :Integer#+, v10
# call to String#+          ...
# call to Array#+           Send v10, :+, v10 # SendFallbackReason: Send: polymorphic fallback
#+end_example
- Ruby 4.1.0-preview1 · default settings

/Say:/

Now the honest part: where ZJIT gives up.

Calm water, only whole numbers: ZJIT splices double in, one check, one add.

Choppy: five types. ZJIT plans for all of them, and every case becomes a
call into C, even whole numbers. YJIT keeps a fast add for whole numbers
and a version per type. In real chop, the swimmer who looks up often beats
the one swimming a planned line. Same here: today, YJIT has the faster
path. ZJIT
still saves the call to double itself. That's this build, today.

[Depth: neither bailed out to the interpreter, 0 side exits each
(captures zjit-choppy-stats, yjit-choppy-stats).]

/Next: Measured: the ZJIT team's results, and ours/

** 22. Measured: the ZJIT team's results, and ours  (17:00, 0:45)

/On screen:/

| What                                      | YJIT    | ZJIT    | Source                      |
|-------------------------------------------+---------+---------+-----------------------------|
| Instance-variable writes (setivar), per run | 5 ms    | 2 ms    | ZJIT team, Mar 2026          |
| JIT memory, Shopify storefront            | 125 MiB | 101 MiB | ZJIT team, Oct 2026          |
| Ruby calls in =params[:name].present?=    | 4       | 0       | ours                        |
| Machine code for our =params= program     | 320 KiB | 352 KiB | ours                        |
| Bail-outs to the interpreter, choppy water | 0       | 0       | ours                        |

- The team, Oct 2026: ZJIT is "probably as fast as or faster than YJIT" on Shopify's storefront, and "there are definitely some where we are worse". Ours are counts and sizes from this talk's captures, not timings.
- Sources: Denbeaux, Rails at Scale, 2026-03-18 · Bernstein, Rails at Scale, 2026-10-09 · ours: captures/ in the repo

/Say:/

Don't take my word for it. Here's what the ZJIT team has measured, next to
what we've seen today.

Theirs: on a benchmark of instance-variable writes, ZJIT is over twice as
fast as YJIT, from an optimization that works across the whole method. On
Shopify's storefront, it uses less memory, and they call it probably as
fast as or faster than YJIT. In their words, there are still some where
it's worse.

Ours are counts, not timings: four calls gone in our params line, no
bail-outs in chop. And ZJIT generated a bit more machine code, which the
team says too.

[Depth: team, Oct 2026: "we generate more code (less precise than LBBV and
more versions) and probably bigger code". Sizes are each compiler's
reported code region (code_region_size / code_region_bytes), captures
hwia-yjit-stats and hwia-zjit-stats.]

** 23. Read your own code  (17:45, 0:30)

/On screen:/
- code:
#+begin_example
ruby -r ./your_file -e 'puts RubyVM::InstructionSequence.of(method(:m)).disasm'
ruby --zjit --zjit-dump-hir   your_file.rb
ruby --zjit --zjit-stats      your_file.rb
#+end_example
- Look for:
- 1. A call that's still a call: a turn you could make easier
- 2. Checks you didn't expect: a value that isn't one type
- 3. Calls into C: time mostly out of the compiler's reach

/Say:/

Three commands: the bytecode, ZJIT's plan, ZJIT's statistics.

In the plan, look for three things. Calls that are still calls. Checks on
values you thought were always one type. And calls into C, where the time
is out of the compiler's reach.

/Next: What it means for Ruby/

** 24. What it means for Ruby  (18:15, 0:45)

/On screen:/
- YJIT compiles Ruby a bit at a time, deciding as it goes; ZJIT plans a
- whole method at once, so it can see through small method calls and pay
- less for them. That's the ceiling the ZJIT team set out to raise.

/Say:/

[Read the slide.]

For you: small, clear methods are exactly what inlining is for. The 4.1
notes list "method inlining" for small Ruby methods.

The 4.0 release notes call ZJIT "the next generation of YJIT", and set the
goal "faster than YJIT and production-ready in Ruby 4.1". The 4.1 notes
say it can still be slower on larger apps. 4.1 ships in a few weeks. Try
it with --zjit.

[Sources: Ruby 4.0.0 release notes, 2025-12-25; Ruby 4.1 NEWS.]
